A table component renders 500 rows via a <Row> child component. Every keystroke in an unrelated search input at the top of the page causes all 500 rows to re-render and visibly stutter, even though the row data hasn't changed. Diagnose the likely cause(s) and describe the fix.

reference_answer.text: The parent re-renders on every keystroke (state lives in the same component tree as the table), and each render creates new inline callback/object props (e.g. onClick={() => ...}) passed to Row, so even a memoized Row sees new prop references and re-renders anyway. Fix by wrapping Row in React.memo, stabilizing callbacks with useCallback and derived objects with useMemo, and/or lifting the search input's state so it doesn't force the table's parent to re-render, plus considering list virtualization for 500 rows.
rubric_points: Identifies that unrelated state colocated with the table forces unnecessary re-renders of the whole subtree
Identifies inline function/object props breaking React.memo reference equality
Proposes React.memo + useCallback/useMemo and/or state colocation/virtualization as the fix

questions.question_text: You're writing a test for a component that calls an API in a useEffect on mount, shows a spinner, then renders the fetched list. Walk through how you'd structure this test with React Testing Library, including how you handle the async gap between the spinner and final render.

reference_answer.text: Mock the network call (e.g. mock the fetch module or an injected client) so the test controls timing and data. Render the component, assert the loading state is present synchronously, then use findByText/findByRole or waitFor to assert the resolved UI, letting RTL handle awaiting the state update instead of manual setTimeout waits. Assert on user-visible output (list items rendered) rather than internal state or implementation details.
rubric_points: Mocks the data-fetching dependency rather than hitting a real network
Uses findBy*/waitFor for the async assertion instead of arbitrary waits or act() misuse
Asserts on rendered output/behavior, not internal implementation details

In the Next.js App Router, which approach produces HTML at build time for a page with no per-request dynamic data, like a static marketing page?

choices.text: Static rendering (the default behavior for pages with no dynamic APIs/data access)
Per-request server rendering triggered by cookies() or headers() usage
Client-side fetching inside a useEffect in a client component

questions.question_text: A Next.js App Router page needs to display stock prices that should feel near-real-time (updating every few seconds) while still loading fast on first paint. Describe the data fetching strategy you'd use for the initial render and the live updates.

reference_answer.text: Server-render the initial page with a fast, cached or short-revalidate fetch (e.g. fetch with a short revalidate window or no-store if freshness matters more than cache hits) so the first paint has real data quickly. Layer live updates on top with a client component that polls an API route or subscribes via WebSocket/SSE after hydration, rather than trying to keep the whole page fully static or fully dynamic on every request.
rubric_points: Server-renders initial content for fast first paint instead of pure client-side fetching
Recognizes full static generation is wrong fit for near-real-time data
Proposes client-side polling or WebSocket/SSE for ongoing updates after hydration

questions.question_text: Design an authentication gate for a Next.js app using edge middleware: certain routes should require a logged-in session, and you want to avoid hitting the database on every request just to check auth.

reference_answer.text: Store a signed session token (e.g. JWT) in an httpOnly cookie set at login. In middleware, verify the token's signature and expiry locally (no DB call) using a fast crypto check, and redirect to /login (preserving the original destination via a query param) if invalid or missing. Scope middleware to only the routes that need protection via the matcher config to avoid unnecessary overhead on public routes. Handle token refresh/expiry via a short-lived access token plus a refresh flow, keeping any DB-backed session revocation checks in the actual route handlers rather than middleware if strict revocation is required.
rubric_points: Verifies a signed token locally in middleware instead of querying the DB per request
Scopes middleware via matcher config to avoid running on unrelated routes
Handles redirect-with-return-url and token expiry/refresh strategy

questions.question_text:
Explain to a teammate what Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) does, and when you'd reach for a revalidate time versus on-demand revalidation.
  Keep it practical, not textbook.

reference_answer.text: ISR lets a statically generated page get regenerated in the background after it goes stale, instead of requiring a full site rebuild — visitors keep getting the old cached page until the new one finishes generating, then future requests get the fresh version. A time-based revalidate (e.g. revalidate: 60) fits content that goes stale predictably (a blog list). On-demand revalidation (triggering revalidation via an API call/webhook) fits content tied to explicit events, like a CMS publish action, where you want freshness immediately rather than waiting out a timer.
rubric_points: Explains background regeneration without a full rebuild, serving stale-then-fresh
Distinguishes time-based revalidate from on-demand/webhook-triggered revalidation
Gives a concrete scenario for when each is the better fit

Return the JSON string of the sum of 'amount' for records where status == 'paid' (return "0" if none match).

This permission check is meant to allow access only if the user is active AND (staff OR the object owner), but an operator precedence bug lets some inactive users through / denies valid staff. Fix it and implement solve(input) in Python. input is a JSON string: {"is_staff": bool, "is_owner": bool, "is_active": bool}. Return "true" or "false" as a JSON string for: is_active AND (is_staff OR is_owner).

Buggy version:

    return is_active and is_staff or is_owner
When you call user.set_password('mypassword') on Django's built-in User model, what determines how the password is hashed and salted before being stored?
A teammate proposes moving expensive shipping-cost calculation logic into a custom Django middleware so it 'runs consistently for every request.' Push back on or defend this design choice.

reference_answer.text: Push back: middleware runs on every request matching its scope regardless of whether that request actually needs shipping calculation, so this wastes CPU on unrelated requests (static asset requests, unrelated API calls, admin pages) and makes an expensive, request-specific computation a global cost. Middleware is meant for cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, CORS, request/response transformation), not business logic tied to a specific feature. The calculation belongs in the view/service layer where it's only invoked when actually needed, with normal caching applied there instead.
rubric_points: Recognizes middleware executes for every matching request, not just relevant ones
Distinguishes cross-cutting concerns (middleware's job) from feature-specific business logic
Recommends the view/service layer as the correct place for the calculation

questions.question_text: Your Django test suite passes locally but intermittently fails in CI with unique-constraint violations or 'database is locked' errors when tests run in parallel. Diagnose the likely causes.

reference_answer.text: Likely causes: tests aren't properly isolated in their own transactions (e.g. using TransactionTestCase where plain TestCase's atomic rollback would have sufficed), shared fixture data or hardcoded IDs/unique fields colliding across parallel workers, or parallel workers sharing a single SQLite file which serializes/locks writes. Fix by preferring TestCase's per-test transaction rollback over TransactionTestCase unless truly needed, using factories with randomized/sequenced unique values instead of hardcoded ones, and ensuring each parallel worker gets its own test database.
rubric_points: Identifies improper test isolation (TransactionTestCase vs TestCase rollback) as a cause
Identifies fixture/unique-field collisions across parallel test runs
Identifies shared database file/connection contention under parallel workers

Implement solve(input) in Python. input is a JSON string: {"path": string}. Return "true" if path matches the pattern '/items/{item_id}' where item_id is a positive integer, else "false".
What's the main practical benefit of injecting a database session into a path operation via Depends() instead of creating the session inline inside the function body?

choices.text: It centralizes session lifecycle management and lets you override the dependency in tests without touching the endpoint code
It makes the endpoint execute faster at runtime
It's required for the endpoint to be declared async
It automatically adds authentication to the route

questions.question_text: An endpoint accepts a nested JSON payload for creating an order with a list of line items, and malformed input should return clear, field-level 422 errors. Describe how you'd model this with Pydantic.

reference_answer.text: Define nested BaseModel classes (e.g. LineItem with sku: str, quantity: conint(gt=0), unit_price: confloat(gt=0), and OrderCreate with customer_id: int and items: List[LineItem] with a min_items constraint). FastAPI automatically returns a 422 with per-field error paths when validation fails, without extra code. Add custom validators (@field_validator/@model_validator) for cross-field rules, like ensuring items isn't empty or totals are consistent.
rubric_points: Uses nested Pydantic models to represent the nested payload structure
Applies field-level constraints (conint/confloat/min_items etc.) rather than manual checks
Mentions FastAPI's automatic 422 field-level error response and/or custom validators for cross-field rules

questions.question_text: A FastAPI endpoint needs to call three independent external APIs and combine the results before responding. Design this endpoint for minimal latency.

reference_answer.text: Declare the endpoint as async def and use an async HTTP client (e.g. httpx.AsyncClient) to issue all three calls concurrently with asyncio.gather instead of awaiting them sequentially. Reuse a single client instance (e.g. via app lifespan/dependency) for connection pooling instead of creating a new client per request. Set per-call timeouts and handle partial failures (e.g. one API failing shouldn't necessarily fail the whole response if a partial result is acceptable). Avoid calling blocking/sync IO libraries inside the async def, since that would block the event loop and negate the concurrency benefit.
rubric_points: Uses asyncio.gather (or equivalent) to run the three calls concurrently rather than sequentially
Reuses a pooled async client instead of creating one per request
Flags the risk of blocking sync calls inside an async endpoint stalling the event loop

questions.question_text: Write a short code-review comment explaining to a junior developer why they should use FastAPI's TestClient with app.dependency_overrides instead of monkeypatching the database module directly to test an endpoint.

reference_answer.text: Something like: 'Instead of monkeypatching the db module globally, use app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = override_get_db for this test. It's scoped to the dependency FastAPI actually injects, so you're testing through the real dependency graph instead of a global patch that can leak into other tests or hide import-order bugs. It's also trivial to reset between tests (dependency_overrides.clear()), which keeps tests independent.'
rubric_points: Explains dependency_overrides targets the actual injected dependency rather than a global patch
Notes the risk of monkeypatch leaking state or being import-order sensitive
Mentions ease of resetting/scoping overrides per test for isolation

questions.question_text: A table has 10 million rows and you run frequent WHERE email = ? lookups with no index on email. What should you expect?

choices.text: A sequential scan of the entire table for each lookup
Postgres auto-creates an index the first time the query runs
Constant-time lookup regardless of table size
The planner refuses to run the query without an index

questions.question_text: Which join returns all rows from the left table plus matched rows from the right table, filling in NULLs where there's no match on the right?

Two concurrent transactions each SELECT a product's stock count, then separately decrement and write it back. Under load, this results in overselling — the stock count ends up higher than it should after both transactions commit. Diagnose the issue and propose a fix.

reference_answer.text: This is a classic lost-update race: both transactions read the same stale stock value before either writes, so the second write overwrites the first decrement instead of compounding it. Fix by locking the row for the duration of the read-modify-write with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or better, avoid the read-then-write pattern entirely with an atomic UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock >= 1, checking the affected row count to detect insufficient stock.
rubric_points: Identifies the lost-update race between concurrent read-then-write operations
Proposes row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or an atomic single-statement UPDATE as the fix
Mentions checking the result (rows affected / stock >= threshold) to detect insufficient stock

questions.question_text: A reporting query joining 4 large tables and aggregating results takes 40 seconds. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows sequential scans on the large tables feeding into nested loop joins. Design an approach to speed this up.

reference_answer.text: Check that filter and join columns have appropriate indexes (the seq scans suggest they don't, or statistics are stale so the planner isn't using them). Run ANALYZE to refresh planner statistics if they're out of date. Once indexed, nested loops on smaller filtered sets are fine, but for genuinely large joins consider whether a hash join would be more appropriate (often means increasing work_mem so it doesn't spill to disk). For a recurring report, consider a materialized view refreshed on a schedule, or table partitioning if the large tables are naturally partitionable (e.g. by date), rather than re-computing the full join every time.
rubric_points: Investigates missing indexes on join/filter columns and stale statistics as root causes
Considers work_mem/hash join tuning for large aggregations
Proposes materialized views or partitioning for a recurring expensive report

questions.question_text: Explain the difference between a UNIQUE constraint and a plain UNIQUE index in Postgres, and why you might explicitly add the constraint even though it creates an index under the hood anyway.

reference_answer.text: A UNIQUE constraint is a schema-level integrity rule that Postgres implements internally using a unique index — so functionally, uniqueness is enforced either way. The reason to declare it as a constraint (not just an index) is intent and tooling: constraints document the business rule explicitly in the schema, participate in features like ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT, and in some contexts (like being the target of a foreign key) Postgres requires an actual unique constraint or primary key rather than just any unique index.
rubric_points: Explains a unique constraint is backed by a unique index under the hood
Notes the constraint communicates schema-level intent versus a bare index
Mentions a practical difference like ON CONFLICT usage or foreign key target requirements

Explain to a teammate the difference between throwing inside an async function and rejecting the returned promise, and how try/catch interacts with await.

reference_answer.text: Throwing inside an async function is automatically converted into a rejected promise — there's no functional difference from explicitly returning Promise.reject(err) from the caller's perspective. When you await a rejected promise inside a try block, the rejection is re-thrown synchronously at that point in the async function, so a normal try/catch around the await catches it just like a sync throw. If you await outside a try/catch (or don't await/handle it at all), the rejection propagates as an unhandled promise rejection instead of being catchable locally.
rubric_points: States that throwing inside async functions produces a rejected promise
Explains await re-throws a rejected promise synchronously so try/catch can catch it
Notes what happens when a rejection isn't awaited/caught (unhandled rejection)

questions.question_text: Write a short code-review comment explaining to a teammate why mixing CommonJS require() and ES module import/export in the same Node.js project is breaking their build, and how to fix it.

reference_answer.text: Something like: 'The build is failing because this file is being treated as CommonJS (no "type": "module" in package.json / .cjs extension) but you're using ESM import/export syntax in it, which Node can't parse under CommonJS rules. Either rename it to .mjs / set "type": "module" in package.json and convert any require() calls to import, or keep it CommonJS and switch back to require()/module.exports. Also watch for interop quirks — importing a CommonJS module from ESM sometimes needs .default depending on how it's exported.'
rubric_points: Identifies the root cause as a module-system mismatch (file being parsed as CJS vs ESM)
Gives a concrete fix (package.json type field / file extension / consistent syntax)
Mentions CJS/ESM interop quirks (e.g. default export access) as a secondary point

questions.question_text: A team is incrementally adding type hints to a large, previously untyped Django/FastAPI codebase and wants CI to catch type errors without rewriting everything at once. Describe your approach.

reference_answer.text: Introduce mypy or pyright with gradual typing rather than flipping strict mode on globally: run it in CI but scope strict checking to new or already-typed modules (e.g. via per-module overrides or a growing allowlist), so untyped legacy code doesn't fail the build. Prioritize adding types to public interfaces/boundaries first (service functions, API schemas) since those give the most value, use Protocol/TypedDict for structural typing where full class hierarchies aren't practical, and track any necessary # type: ignore usages so they don't silently accumulate.
rubric_points: Proposes gradual/incremental typing via per-module config rather than global strict mode
Prioritizes typing public interfaces/boundaries over the whole codebase at once
Mentions tracking or limiting type: ignore usage to avoid silent accumulation

questions.question_text: A teammate wants to pin every transitive dependency to an exact version (using pip freeze output as requirements.txt) for a library package they're about to publish to PyPI. Defend or push back on this.

reference_answer.text: Push back for a library: exact-pinning transitive dependencies forces every downstream consumer to accept those exact versions too, which causes dependency resolution conflicts the moment two libraries in someone's project pin incompatible exact versions of the same transitive dependency. Libraries should declare loose, compatible version ranges (e.g. requests>=2.28,<3) so pip's resolver has room to satisfy the whole dependency graph. Exact pinning via a lockfile is the right call for a deployable application (where reproducibility across environments matters more than composability), and tools like pip-tools or Poetry can keep that distinction between published constraints and a dev lockfile.
rubric_points: Identifies exact transitive pinning in a library causing downstream dependency resolution conflicts
Distinguishes library version-range constraints from application lockfile pinning
Recommends compatible version ranges and/or a tool that separates constraints from lockfiles

questions.question_text: Adding an index speeds up SELECT queries filtering on that column, but tends to slow down which kind of operation?

choices.text: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, since the index must also be maintained on every write

questions.question_text: A CROSS JOIN between a table with 100 rows and a table with 50 rows, with no filtering, produces how many rows?

Under load, the application starts throwing 'deadlock detected' errors. Two different endpoints each update the same two tables, but in opposite order, within their transactions. Diagnose the cause and propose a fix.

reference_answer.text: This is a classic deadlock from inconsistent lock acquisition order: transaction A locks table1 then waits on table2, while transaction B locks table2 then waits on table1, and neither can proceed. Fix by enforcing a consistent ordering for acquiring locks/updating tables across all code paths that touch both tables, keeping transactions short to reduce the lock window, and adding retry-with-backoff logic for the (still possible) occasional deadlock rather than assuming it can be eliminated entirely.
rubric_points: Identifies inconsistent lock/update ordering across transactions as the deadlock cause
Proposes enforcing a consistent ordering across all code paths as the primary fix
Mentions shortening transactions and/or retry-with-backoff as a complementary mitigation

questions.question_text: You need to diagnose and fix a slow production report query, but you only have read access to a query log and EXPLAIN, and can't take a full outage window. Design your approach.

reference_answer.text: Reproduce the query with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) against a staging replica with representative data volume rather than against production directly, so you're not adding load to prod while investigating. Look for sequential scans and high-cost nodes on large tables, check whether relevant filter/join columns are indexed, and confirm table statistics are current (stale stats can make the planner choose bad plans even with indexes present). If a new index is needed, create it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production to avoid locking the table, then re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE afterward to confirm the plan actually improved before considering it done.
rubric_points: Reproduces and analyzes the query plan on staging/replica rather than live production
Looks for missing indexes and stale statistics as root causes via EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Uses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (or equivalent non-locking approach) and verifies the fix with a before/after plan comparison

questions.question_text: A product manager asks why the engineering team wants to split a single wide 'orders' table (which repeats the customer's address on every order row) into separate 'orders' and 'customers' tables, given the current setup 'already works.' Explain the trade-off in plain, non-technical terms.

reference_answer.text: Right now, if a customer's address changes, we'd have to update it on every single order row for that customer, and if we miss even one, our records disagree with each other about where that customer lives — that's the real risk, not just tidiness. Splitting the data so each customer's address lives in exactly one place means an update happens once and every order automatically reflects the correct, current address. The trade-off is that looking up an order's shipping details now requires joining two tables instead of reading one, which is a small, well-understood cost compared to the risk of inconsistent data as the business grows.
rubric_points: Explains the redundancy/update-anomaly risk of repeating address data per order in plain terms
Explains normalization gives a single source of truth for the address
Acknowledges the join-cost trade-off honestly rather than pretending there's no downside
